entry.title: Software 3.0 - AI & Agentic Engineering for SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 Development
entry.content:
Agentic AI can now produce a working SAPUI5 application in hours rather than weeks.

The engineering question is no longer whether an agent can write the code, but how a Fiori development team keeps that speed inside enterprise design, data and release discipline. 

 A recent SAP Community article, “How to use the new Google IDE Antigravity with SAP (and CAP)”, provides a useful prelude to this discussion. It shows how an agent-first development environment can be connected to the SAP ecosystem: install Node.js and the development kit, configure SAP extensions, and expose project context through an MCP server. 

The toolchain used throughout this walkthrough: SAPUI5 in Google AntiGravity. 

But installing an agentic IDE is only the beginning. The more important question is this: what does it mean, to engineer a production-grade SAP Fiori application when agents such as Claude and Gemini can already generate a full SAPUI5 application that follows SAP Fiori design guidelines and best practices? These agents no longer stop at generation. They inspect the repository, edit several files at once, run the application against mock data, observe failures and revise their own work.

The definition of development work is changing. 

This article sets out a step-by-step path for using agentic coding to build SAPUI5 applications. The method is not theoretical — it has produced thousands of lines of code across several SAPUI5 Fiori applications, running in production. Each step is illustrated with numbered screenshots from that work, so the method can be verified. 

By the end of this article you will be able to scaffold a SAPUI5 project with SAP Fiori tools, brief an agent against the SAP Fiori Design Guidelines, validate the screen with mock data, map every binding to OData metadata, prove the application under realistic system load, and release it through a governed transport.

 

Software 3.0 changes the Fiori software development lifecycle at its core.

In the agentic era, the Fiori expert defines the experience and the guardrails, uses SAP Fiori tools to establish the project correctly, and treats an AI agent such as Google Antigravity or Claude Code as an implementation partner that can plan, edit, run, inspect and refine the application. This article follows that workflow in Google Antigravity, which Google describes as an “agent-first development platform” where agents plan, execute and verify complex work across the editor, terminal and browser, and where tangible artifacts such as implementation plans, browser controls and screenshots make the work easy for a human to verify.

The Core idea is to have production-ready SAPUI5 Fiori application, moving through six controlled stages: scaffold, prompt, simulate, map, load-test, and release.

The working model is simple. Start with SAP Fiori Guided Development, let the agent generate and refine the UI, and validate it with mock data. Map every binding against the OData metadata and the underlying Virtual Data Model (VDM), the CDS-based model that an S/4HANA service exposes. Then prove the application under realistic system load before moving it to production.

This makes Software 3.0 tangible for Fiori: the human defines the business outcome, architecture and guardrails, while the agent performs the fast paced implementation, testing, debugging and iteration.

 

A. From Software 1.0 to Software 3.0

A useful way to think about the evolution is to ask how the developer programs in today's era. 

 

Era

Primary programming mechanism

Developer focus

Software 1.0

Hand-written code

Statements, functions, algorithms

Software 2.0

Auto-complete, Code generation, Pair Programming

Data, objective, logic.

Software 3.0 (Since early 2026 onwards)

Natural-language instructions + AI agents

Context, architecture, constraints, verification

 

New Development Plan: Requirement -> Architect -> Agent Plan -> Multi-file Implementation -> Diff Checks -> Runtime Verification -> Agentic PRs/ Release

The result is a different development loop. Instead of write, run, debug and repeat, the cycle becomes state the intent, review the agent's plan, let it implement across files, then check diffs and the runtime evidence it returns. The developer's time moves from typing the change to judging whether the change is right.

 

B. The Six-Step Agentic Fiori Method

The Agentic UI5 development model deliberately separates Fiori element design, frontend implementation, system testing, and production governance. That separation is what prevents a fast prototype from becoming an ungoverned production change.

 

Stage

Human owns

Agent accelerates

Evidence before moving on

1. Create the foundation

App scope, Fiori floorplan, service target

Project files, manifests, initial views

A runnable Freestyle project with a clear file structure

2. Prompt the UI5 implementation

Fiori Design Guidelines, responsive behaviour, naming rules

Multi-file XML/JS/i18n/CSS changes and refactoring, logic builds

Diff review, design checklist, and a working local preview

3. Test with mock data

Scenarios, edge cases, expected states

Mock data generation, loading states, error cases

Repeatable local tests with metadata-accurate responses

4. Map XML OData metadata

VDM/service semantics, key fields, associations, business rules

Entity-to-control mapping and binding scaffolding

A mapping table, validated bindings

5. Move into SAP Business Application Studio for full-system testing

Test scope, destinations, authorizations, performance thresholds

Test harnesses, scripts, diagnostics, and remediation proposals

System-level test results and resolved defects

6. Implement in production

Approval, security, transport, rollout, support

Build checks, release notes, deployment assistance

Approved artifact deployed to Production via the Transport and App visible through the intended launchpad path

 

 

C. Walkthrough: the six steps in practice

Before working through the six steps, lets put the baseline in place. You need Node.js with the UI5 tooling; SAP Fiori tools (Application Wizard, Guided Development and Service Modeler) in Visual Studio Code or SAP Business Application Studio; an agentic IDE such as Google Antigravity; a development OData service, or a saved copy of its $metadata document; and a destination or transport path to the target system. Every step below assumes this baseline exists. 

Figure 1. SAP UI5  tools in NPM package

 

1. Create a Freestyle Fiori application with Fiori Guided Development

Start with the SAP-aware foundation instead of asking an agent to invent a UI5 project structure. SAP Fiori tools in Visual Studio Code gives you three things you need in sequence: an Application Wizard that generates both SAP Fiori elements and freestyle SAPUI5 templates, Guided Development that applies supported how-to guidance for adding functionality, and a Service Modeler that lets you inspect the OData metadata behind the service, including entities, properties and associations. This matters because the wizard produces the layout, manifest and build configuration that SAP itself supports, so the agent works inside a structure the platform can run, test and deploy.

The accurate working pattern is therefore: use the Application Wizard to create the Freestyle SAPUI5 project, then use Guided Development and the Fiori Tools modelers to establish supported patterns.

The initial project should contain a predictable structure: manifest.json, Component.js, XML views, controllers, fragments, i18n resources, models, test folders, and a localService area for mock assets.

·      SAP Fiori Tools

 

·      SAP Fiori Generator

 

 

·      Template Selection: Use Upload a Metadata Document

Figure 2. Guided Development in SAP Fiori tools: the supported how-to guide selected for this application, and the generated code step it applies to the project.

 

·      Running through the option in Guided Development: The complexity increases - Then it is time to invoke the Agents.

 

Figure 3. Guided Development in SAP Fiori tools and AI Agents: the supported how-to guide selected for this application, and the generated code step it applies to the project.

 

·      Final Base SAP Fiori UI5 Program Structure

 

Figure 4. The base freestyle SAPUI5 project generated by the SAP Fiori tools Application Wizard, showing manifest.json, Component.js, XML views, controllers, fragments, i18n resources, models, test folders and the localService area for mock assets.

 

2. Prompt the UI5 implementation against SAP Fiori Design Guidelines

Open the generated codebase in the agentic IDE ie Google Antigravity. Now-forth, we will use Natural language for Prompting and will bring  the required features to existence. The quality of an agentic result depends on the quality of the context you give it. Do not prompt with “build me a dashboard.” Give Antigravity a structured brief: the business task and the persona it serves,  the entity sets and fields to bind, the files it may touch, the conventions it must obey, and the checks that must pass before it reports back.

This is where SAP Fiori expertise matters most. The agent should be instructed to preserve responsive behavior, clear information hierarchy, meaningful empty and busy states, content density, internationalization and semantic status colors. It should also understand that XML views, controllers, formatters, manifest.json, and i18n.properties form one coordinated change rather than six unrelated files. This is where the "TASTE" of the developer/Functional Profession matters in designing the UX.

 

·      Prompting and Agent Capability Examples

The screenshots that follow run through two agents: Codex and Google Antigravity. They are included as documentary evidence of the overall Agent engineering features described above - the brief, the implementation plan, the multi-file diff, the run against mock data, and the correction that followed - rather than as a comparison of the two products.

·      Codex Agent

Figure 5. A Codex session on the same repository: the task brief given to the agent, the files it selected to change, and the implementation it proposed before any code was written to disk.

 

·      Anti-Gravity Agentic Development IDE

In Google Antigravity, heavily rely on /grill-me mode to clarify that the Agent has understood the Feature requirements correctly before proceeding. This is the most important as "Tokens" are as good as "Cash" these days. !

Figure 6. The Google Antigravity agent harness: the implementation plan produced before any file is changed, alongside the editor, terminal and browser surfaces the agent works across.

 

·      Code Diff checks

Figure 7. The multi-file diff returned by the agent, covering the XML view, controller, manifest.json and i18n resources as one coordinated change rather than four unrelated edits.

 

 

·      Code Performance review by Agents

Figure 8. An agent-run performance review of the UI5 implementation, listing the issues found in the generated code and the correction proposed for each.

 

 

·      UI5 Fiori Elements logic implementation

 

Figure 9. SAP Fiori elements logic implemented by the agent, showing how the described business task was turned into a working view and controller.

 

·      Fiori Elements – Few Examples created by Agents

 

·      Inverted Status

 

·      Progress Line Bar Inline Graph

 

·      Delta Graph%

 

·      Harvey Inline Micro-chart

Figure 10. The generated SAP Fiori elements screens rendered in the running application, showing the floorplan, list behaviour and semantic status colours prescribed in the brief.

 

·      Fiori Application Errors during development - Solved by AI Agents

Figure 11. Errors raised by the Fiori application during development, captured from the console and network output that the agent uses as the input to its debugging loop.

 

·      Anti-Gravity Browser based Automated Testing Loop for Agentic Debugging of Errors

The Most Important features of Google Antigravity is the /goal Mode and the Browser based Self- Testing.

 

Figure 12. The Antigravity browser-based test loop: the agent runs the application, reads the browser and network output, revises the code and repeats until the scenario passes, returning the run as a reviewable artifact.

 

·      Software Debugging – Agentic Workflow for Root cause Analysis

Figure 13. The agentic root-cause analysis workflow, tracing a failure from the symptom observed in the browser back to the responsible binding and the code change that introduced it.

 

The operating rule is plan first, edit second, verify continuously. Ask the agent to produce an implementation plan before it changes files. Review the plan for scope and architecture. Then let it make a small, coherent change, run the local application, inspect console and browser output. A short cycle is safer than one enormous prompt that changes the entire repository.

 

3. Test with a mock-data generator

A Fiori screen should become testable before it depends on a live SAP backend.  A Mock Server simulates a backend from local service metadata and mock data, allowing developers to test without depending on the availability of the real service or adding load to the system where the service runs. 

Use the mock stage to generate synthetic data that mirrors the shape of production: full result sets and empty ones, long texts and null values, boundary dates, large numbers, every status value the UI colour-codes. 

 

Figure 14. Mock data generated from the service metadata and served by the SAPUI5 Mock Server, covering full result sets, empty results, long texts, null values, boundary dates and every status value the UI colour-codes.

Prompt Antigravity to add or vary data one scenario at a time. Then ask it to run the mock page, capture the rendered result and report what each scenario proves. This turns mock data into a repeatable visual regression check you can run again after every change.

 

4. Use XML OData metadata for VDM and OData mapping logic

The XML document available at the service’s /$metadata endpoint is useful. It is not a substitute for domain knowledge, but it is the reliable starting point for the Agent to mapp the frontend to the backend. For SAP S/4HANA scenarios, the service may represent data from a CDS-based Virtual Data Model. The frontend agent must consume what the service actually exposes.

Figure 15. The OData $metadata document inspected in the SAP Fiori tools Service Modeler, showing the entity sets, keys, properties, associations and annotations used to validate every binding in the application.

 

·      SAPUI5 Fiori UI/UX Experience- Created by SAPUI5 AI Agentic Engineering

  • UX - STAGE 1 (Initial Prompting)

 

  •  UX - FINAL STAGE (Multiple Rounds of Prompting)

Figure 16. A sample snip of a SAPUI5 Fiori application A Custom Project Management Dashboard with Agentic Development

 

·      KPIs Tiles – Created by SAPUI5 Agentic Engineering

Note that 

·      Sample Purchase Order Overview Dashboard with superior UI/UX – Created by SAPUI5 AI Agentic Engineering

Figure 17. Sample KPIs and SAPUI5 Fiori Applications created in Google AntiGravity with agentic engineering, rendered in the finished application with superior UI/UX (Represented here with Anonymised Mock Data only)

Note that till that we are operating in Local Development, only.

 

5. Move the application into SAP Business Application Studio for full-system, authorization and load testing

The fifth step moves the application from a local, metadata-driven prototype into an environment where its end-to-end assumptions can be tested. SAP Business Application Studio is an appropriate development and deployment environment for SAP Fiori projects.

The practical sequence is:

  • Import or clone the UI5 project into SAP BAS and confirm that the generated project runs without the local-only assumptions hidden by the prototype.
  • Run functional tests, including authorization failures, empty results, long-running reads, paging, optimistic concurrency, and backend errors.
  • Run performance and load tests at the system boundary. Measure browser rendering, request latency, payload size, Gateway and backend resource consumption. Do not treat a local mock test as a load test.

 

6. Implement in production

Production implementation is a governed release. Before release, the team should confirm that the build is reproducible, unit and integration tests have passed, the app meets accessibility and responsive requirements,  security and authorization behaviour is understood and the target SAPUI5/runtime version is compatible.

·      Preparing for Production

Figure 18. Production readiness evidence: build, test and configuration checks collected and reviewed before the change was submitted for release approval.

The final production checklist should cover the target deployment landscape, package and transport details, destination and authentication configuration, versioning, launchpad intent and role assignment, monitoring, rollback, and support ownership. The agent can prepare release notes, documentation, deployment checklists, and test evidence. 

 

Agent SKILLS: fiori_SKILLS.md

There is a major difference between "Let an AI build my Fiori app" and "Let an engineering agent build my Fiori app according to my enterprise architecture." The difference is context.

fiori_SKILLS.md is a production-oriented knowledge base and operating manual for AI coding agents working on SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 code. The Fiori_SKILLS.md captures what an agent cannot infer from the code alone:

  • Identity — application metadata, namespaces, OData services and entity mappings.
  • Structure — the UI model, the frontend architecture, and the files an agent may and may not modify.
  • Craft — coding conventions, reusable implementation playbooks, and the anti-patterns already ruled out on this project.
  • Proof — testing standards, performance constraints and the deployment rules a change must satisfy before release.

fiori_SKILLS.md carries the project architecture, naming conventions, accepted patterns, performance limits and safe modification boundaries into every agent session, so the same rules apply on the hundredth prompt as on the first. Without it, each session starts again from generic training knowledge and the guardrails have to be retyped by hand.

 

D. The operating model: Architect,  System & Agent 

Agentic development works when responsibilities are explicit. The SAP Fiori expert owns user experience, enterprise constraints, data semantics, architectural trade-offs, and release decisions. Google Antigravity coordinates implementation work across the editor, terminal, and browser and produces reviewable artifacts. SAP tooling and the target system provide the supported project model, service contract, runtime behaviour, authorization boundaries, deployment process, and production evidence.

Responsibility

Human architect/developer

Agentic AI

SAP platform/tooling

Experience

Define persona, task, hierarchy, and Fiori pattern

Generate candidate XML and styling changes

Provide supported controls and design-system behaviour

Code

Review diffs and approve architecture

Edit related files, refactor, and test locally

Build and run the UI5 project

Data

Interpret VDM/service semantics and business rules

Inventory metadata and propose bindings

Expose OData metadata, annotations, and responses

Quality

Set acceptance criteria and approve evidence

Run repeatable checks and explain failures

Provide mock server, test, destination, and environment capabilities

Release

Approve change, security, transport, and rollout

Prepare artifacts and release notes

Deploy and integrate with launchpad/runtime

The discipline: Never allow - speed of the Agent to outrun evidence in the browser or the deployment pipeline.

 

E.  Conclusion: Teach the AI Agent "The Method", Not Just the Prompt

Google Antigravity provides an environment in which the AI agent can plan, edit, execute and verify. SAP Fiori Guided Development provides the initial application structure. XML OData metadata and VDM information provide authoritative backend context. Mock data provides a fast feedback loop. BAS backed testing provides the bridge to realistic system validation.

 

Figure 19. A list of AI Agents available in Google Antigravity, which can be leveraged for SAP Fiori UI5 Agentic Coding. The models are getting more powerful with each passing week.

 

Software 3.0 pattern for SAPUI5 Fiori Development:

-- " Teach the agent the architecture, give it the right system context, verify diffs and every result against browser load evidence, rather than against the prompt..."

The practical promise of agentic engineering in the SAP Fiori world: from “Months” of manual efforts to  “only to a Few Weeks” of Human supervised, AI-Agent driven work.

 

The Future is the Agentic Way...! 🤖🤖

entry.title: Generic Excel Upload in SAP CAP (Node.js): Reusable Validation & Row-Level Error Reporting
entry.content:
A few weeks ago I got tired of writing the same Excel-import boilerplate for the third time on a project — parse the sheet, loop the rows, hand-check a bunch of fields, insert whatever survives. Every entity ended up with its own copy-pasted upload handler that only that one screen used. This post walks through a small CAP (Node.js) service I built to fix that: one generic upload action that any entity can reuse, with row-level validation and a proper error report instead of a single "something went wrong" toast.

The full source is a working CAP + Fiori Elements-flavoured UI5 app, and everything below is lifted straight from it — nothing simplified for the blog.

What We're Building

The idea is simple: a user picks an entity from a dropdown, uploads an .xlsx file, and the backend:

  • Parses the workbook and reads the first sheet as JSON rows
  • Validates every row against rules defined for that entity
  • Inserts only the rows that pass validation
  • Returns a structured summary — total rows, success count, error count, and the exact row/field/message for every failure
  • Logs the whole attempt (file name, counts, and the error list as JSON) to an UploadLogs table, so there's an audit trail

The "generic" part is that none of this logic is hard-coded to a single entity. Adding a new importable entity is a matter of adding one object to a rules map — no new controller, no new action, no copy-pasted handler.

Project Structure

Nothing exotic here — a standard CAP layout with one Fiori Elements-generated app on top:

Here is the code of the project structure file:

1. The Data Model

Two entities. Employees is the table we're importing into. UploadLogs is what gives us the audit trail — every upload attempt, successful or not, leaves a record.

Here is the code of schema.cds file:

namespace demo.excelupload;

entity Employees {
  key ID     : Integer;
      name   : String(100);
      email  : String(100);
      salary : Decimal(10,2);
}

entity UploadLogs {
  key uploadId     : UUID;
      fileName     : String(200);
      entityName   : String(100);
      totalRows    : Integer;
      successCount : Integer;
      errorCount   : Integer;
      errors       : LargeString;   // stored as JSON string
      uploadedAt   : Timestamp @CDS.on.insert: $now;
}

The errors field is worth calling out: rather than modeling a separate association/composition for row errors, I just store the array as a JSON string in a LargeString. For a log table you read back and display as-is, that's a lot less ceremony than a child entity, and it keeps the log write to a single INSERT.

2. Exposing It: service.cds

The service exposes both entities as plain projections, plus one bound-free action — uploadExcel — that does the actual work. This is deliberately an action, not an entity CREATE, because a single call needs to return a structured, multi-row result (counts + a list of errors), which doesn't map cleanly onto a normal OData create response.

Here is the code of service.cds file:

using demo.excelupload as db from '../db/schema';
 
service ExcelUploadService {
 
  entity Employees   as projection on db.Employees;
  entity UploadLogs  as projection on db.UploadLogs;
 
  action uploadExcel(
    entityName : String,
    fileName   : String,
    file       : LargeBinary
  ) returns {
    totalRows    : Integer;
    successCount : Integer;
    errorCount   : Integer;
    errors       : array of {
      row     : Integer;
      field   : String;
      message : String;
    };
  };
 
}

entityName tells the handler which target table to insert into and which validation rules to apply. The file itself travels as base64-encoded LargeBinary in the request body — no multipart handling needed, which keeps the UI5 side (below) to a plain fetch() call.

3. The Core Logic: service.js

This is the part that actually makes the thing generic. Everything upload-specific for an entity lives in one small config object:

Here is the code of service.js (validation rules) file:

const VALIDATION_RULES = {
  Employees: {
    name:   { required: true },
    email:  { required: true, type: 'email' },
    salary: { required: true, type: 'number', min: 0 }
  }
};

To onboard a new entity for upload, that's the only entity-specific code you write — a rules object. Everything else (parsing, looping, inserting, logging) is shared.

The generic row validator

validateRow() takes a row and a rules object and doesn't know or care which entity it's validating. It checks required fields first, then type-specific rules (email format, numeric, minimum value) — but only if the field actually has a value, so a missing-but-optional field doesn't also get penalised for "not being a number":

Here is the code of service.js (validateRow function) file:

function validateRow(row, rules) {
  const rowErrors = [];
 
  for (const field in rules) {
    const rule = rules[field];
    const value = row[field];
 
    if (rule.required && (value === undefined || value === null || value === '')) {
      rowErrors.push({ field, message: `${field} is required` });
      continue; // skip further checks on this field if it's missing
    }
 
    if (value !== undefined && value !== null && value !== '') {
      if (rule.type === 'email' && !/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(value)) {
        rowErrors.push({ field, message: `${field} must be a valid email` });
      }
      if (rule.type === 'number' && isNaN(Number(value))) {
        rowErrors.push({ field, message: `${field} must be a number` });
      }
      if (rule.type === 'number' && rule.min !== undefined && Number(value) < rule.min) {
        rowErrors.push({ field, message: `${field} cannot be less than ${rule.min}` });
      }
    }
  }
 
  return rowErrors;
}

It's intentionally basic — required, email, number, min. That's enough to cover most master-data imports, and it's easy to extend with a max, a regex rule, or a custom() function per field if a real project needs it.

The uploadExcel handler

The handler itself reads top to bottom as a checklist. Worth noting: the entity name coming in from the client is validated against this.entities before it's used for anything, so you can't point the action at an arbitrary CDS entity that happens to exist in the model but was never meant to be imported into.

Here is the code of service.js (uploadExcel handler) file:

module.exports = class ExcelUploadService extends cds.ApplicationService {
 
  async init() {
 
    this.on('uploadExcel', async req => {
      const { entityName, fileName, file } = req.data;
 
      // 1. Validate the target entity exists in this service
      const targetEntity = this.entities[entityName];
      if (!targetEntity) {
        return req.error(400, `Unknown entity: ${entityName}`);
      }
 
      // 2. Look up validation rules for this entity (generic lookup)
      const rules = VALIDATION_RULES[entityName];
      if (!rules) {
        return req.error(400, `No validation rules defined for entity: ${entityName}`);
      }
 
      // 3. Ensure we have an actual Buffer before parsing
      const fileBuffer = Buffer.isBuffer(file) ? file : Buffer.from(file, 'base64');
 
      // 4. Parse the Excel file
      const workbook = XLSX.read(fileBuffer, { type: 'buffer' });
      const sheetName = workbook.SheetNames[0];
      const sheet = workbook.Sheets[sheetName];
      const rows = XLSX.utils.sheet_to_json(sheet);
 
      // 5. Validate every row using the generic validator
      const validRows = [];
      const errors = [];
 
      rows.forEach((row, index) => {
        const rowNum = index + 2; // +2 = header row + 1-based index
        const rowErrors = validateRow(row, rules);
 
        if (rowErrors.length > 0) {
          rowErrors.forEach(e => errors.push({ row: rowNum, field: e.field, message: e.message }));
        } else {
          validRows.push(row);
        }
      });
 
      // 6. Insert valid rows only
      if (validRows.length > 0) {
        await INSERT.into(targetEntity).entries(validRows);
      }
 
      // 7. Log the upload attempt
      await INSERT.into('ExcelUploadService.UploadLogs').entries({
        fileName,
        entityName,
        totalRows: rows.length,
        successCount: validRows.length,
        errorCount: errors.length,
        errors: JSON.stringify(errors)
      });
 
      // 8. Return structured summary
      return {
        totalRows: rows.length,
        successCount: validRows.length,
        errorCount: errors.length,
        errors
      };
    });
 
    return super.init();
  }
};

A couple of details that matter more than they look:

  • Row numbers (rowNum = index + 2) are calculated so the error list matches what the user actually sees in Excel — row 1 is the header, so the first data row is row 2. Reporting index (0-based, no header) would send someone to the wrong row every single time.
  • Valid rows are inserted in a single batched INSERT.into(...).entries(validRows) rather than row-by-row — much cheaper than N individual inserts, and it means partial success (some rows in, some rejected) still happens in one round trip to the DB.
  • The UploadLogs write happens unconditionally, even when errorCount is 0 or successCount is 0 — every attempt is logged, not just the ones that partially failed.

4. The UI Layer

The Fiori app is a plain custom page (View1), not a List Report — an upload screen doesn't really benefit from the standard List Report/Object Page scaffolding, so I kept it to a Panel with a FileUploader, an entity Select, and a results table that only appears once there's something to show.

Here is the code of View1.view.xml file:

<mvc:View
    controllerName="project1.controller.View1"
    xmlns="sap.m"
    xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc"
    xmlns:core="sap.ui.core"
    xmlns:u="sap.ui.unified">

    <Page id="page" title="Generic Excel Upload Demo">
        <content>

            <Panel headerText="Upload" class="sapUiResponsiveMargin">
                <content>
                    <VBox class="sapUiSmallMargin">

                        <Label text="Target Entity"/>
                        <Select id="entitySelect" selectedKey="Employees" width="200px">
                            <core:Item key="Employees" text="Employees"/>
                        </Select>

                        <Label text="Excel File (.xlsx)" class="sapUiTinyMarginTop"/>
                        <u:FileUploader
                            id="fileUploader"
                            width="100%"
                            placeholder="Choose a file..."
                            fileType="xlsx"
                            change="onFileChange"/>

                        <Button
                            text="Upload"
                            type="Emphasized"
                            press="onUploadPress"
                            class="sapUiSmallMarginTop"
                            id="uploadBtn"/>

                        <Text id="statusText" class="sapUiTinyMarginTop"/>

                    </VBox>
                </content>
            </Panel>

            <Panel headerText="Upload Result" class="sapUiResponsiveMargin" visible="{ui>/resultVisible}">
                <content>
                    <VBox class="sapUiSmallMargin">

                        <HBox class="sapUiSmallMarginBottom">
                            <ObjectStatus title="Total" text="{ui>/totalRows}" class="sapUiSmallMarginEnd"/>
                            <ObjectStatus title="Success" text="{ui>/successCount}" state="Success" class="sapUiSmallMarginEnd"/>
                            <ObjectStatus title="Errors" text="{ui>/errorCount}" state="Error"/>
                        </HBox>

                        <Table id="errorTable" items="{ui>/errors}">
                            <columns>
                                <Column><Text text="Row"/></Column>
                                <Column><Text text="Field"/></Column>
                                <Column><Text text="Message"/></Column>
                            </columns>
                            <items>
                                <ColumnListItem>
                                    <cells>
                                        <Text text="{ui>row}"/>
                                        <Text text="{ui>field}"/>
                                        <Text text="{ui>message}"/>
                                    </cells>
                                </ColumnListItem>
                            </items>
                        </Table>

                    </VBox>
                </content>
            </Panel>

        </content>
    </Page>
</mvc:View>

The controller does three things: read the picked file as base64 (FileReader.readAsDataURL, then strip the data: prefix), POST it to the action, and push the response into a local JSON model that the results Panel is bound to:

Here is the code of View1.controller.js file:

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/mvc/Controller",
    "sap/ui/model/json/JSONModel",
    "sap/m/MessageToast"
], (Controller, JSONModel, MessageToast) => {
    "use strict";

    return Controller.extend("project1.controller.View1", {

        onInit() {
            const oUIModel = new JSONModel({
                resultVisible: false,
                totalRows: 0,
                successCount: 0,
                errorCount: 0,
                errors: []
            });
            this.getView().setModel(oUIModel, "ui");
            this._selectedFile = null;
        },

        onFileChange(oEvent) {
            const oFiles = oEvent.getParameter("files");
            this._selectedFile = oFiles && oFiles.length ? oFiles[0] : null;
        },

        async onUploadPress() {
            const oView = this.getView();
            const oUIModel = oView.getModel("ui");
            const sEntity = oView.byId("entitySelect").getSelectedKey();
            const oStatusText = oView.byId("statusText");

            if (!this._selectedFile) {
                MessageToast.show("Please choose a file first.");
                return;
            }

            oStatusText.setText("Uploading...");
            oUIModel.setProperty("/resultVisible", false);

            try {
                const sBase64 = await this._fileToBase64(this._selectedFile);
                const sServiceUrl = "/odata/v4/excel-upload/";

                const response = await fetch(sServiceUrl + "uploadExcel", {
                    method: "POST",
                    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
                    body: JSON.stringify({
                        entityName: sEntity,
                        fileName: this._selectedFile.name,
                        file: sBase64
                    })
                });

                const data = await response.json();

                if (!response.ok) {
                    MessageToast.show("Error: " + (data.error?.message || "Upload failed"));
                    oStatusText.setText("");
                    return;
                }

                oUIModel.setData({
                    resultVisible: true,
                    totalRows: data.totalRows,
                    successCount: data.successCount,
                    errorCount: data.errorCount,
                    errors: data.errors || []
                });

                oStatusText.setText("");
                MessageToast.show("Upload complete.");

            } catch (err) {
                MessageToast.show("Unexpected error: " + err.message);
                oStatusText.setText("");
            }
        },

        _fileToBase64(oFile) {
            return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
                const reader = new FileReader();
                reader.onload = () => {
                    const sBase64 = reader.result.split(",")[1];
                    resolve(sBase64);
                };
                reader.onerror = reject;
                reader.readAsDataURL(oFile);
            });
        }

    });
});

I went with a plain fetch() to the action's OData path rather than wiring this through the OData V4 model's callFunction/invoke API. For a single action with a binary payload, the model API adds more indirection than it saves — this way the base64 conversion and the request are both fully in my control, and it's obvious from reading the controller exactly what's going over the wire.

5. Trying It Out

With the app running (cds watch), an .xlsx with columns name, email, salary and a mix of valid and deliberately broken rows (a blank email, a negative salary, a non-numeric salary) produces exactly what you'd expect: the valid rows land in Employees, and the results panel lists every rejected row with the row number, the offending field, and why it failed — so the person fixing the file doesn't have to guess.

Every attempt — success or partial failure — also shows up as a new row in UploadLogs, with the error list preserved as JSON. That's been genuinely useful even outside the demo: when someone asks "did my file from yesterday actually go in?", the answer is one query away instead of a shrug.

6. Extending to More Entities

Since the whole point was to avoid a one-off handler per entity, adding a second importable entity is three small, additive changes and zero changes to the handler itself:

  • Add the entity to db/schema.cds
  • Expose it as a projection in service.cds
  • Add its field rules to VALIDATION_RULES in service.js

The uploadExcel action, the validateRow() function, the batching, and the logging are all shared as-is. That's the whole value proposition of building it this way instead of one action per entity.

Conclusion

None of the individual pieces here are complicated — parsing a workbook, looping rows, an INSERT. What actually removes the repeated work is keeping the entity-specific bit (the rules) completely separate from the entity-agnostic bit (parse → validate → insert → log), so the second, third, and tenth entity you need to import cost you a rules object instead of a new handler.

A few things I'd add before calling this production-ready: a max file size / row count check before parsing (a 200MB spreadsheet will parse just fine into a very unhappy Node process), a dry-run mode that validates without inserting, and pulling VALIDATION_RULES out of code and into a config entity so business users could adjust required fields without a redeploy. All reasonable next posts.

If you end up building something similar, or have a cleaner approach to the row-error reporting, I'd genuinely like to hear about it in the comments.

 

Thank You

entry.title: SAP UI Integration Cards: Choosing the Right Development Path for Supplier Portals
entry.content:
Supplier Portal projects keep finding their way onto my calendar. Across industries, such as manufacturing, retail, energy, public sector, the pattern repeats: a company runs SAP in the back office, has hundreds or thousands of external suppliers, and needs to give those suppliers a meaningful digital touchpoint without onboarding them into the core system. SAP BTP, and specifically SAP Build Work Zone, is increasingly the answer. If I had to pick a top-5 use case for BTP, this is on the list and the reason is almost always the same: you need to give people outside your company controlled, identity-aware access to your processes. That is a non-trivial problem, and BTP is well-positioned to solve it cleanly.

What I also enjoy about this topic is how many technology layers it touches at once. Identity and access management, OData APIs, low-code tooling, process automation, UI frameworks, a Supplier Portal brings them all into play. It is one of those projects where a good architect genuinely has to think across the stack.

I am also speaking at the SAP Exploration Workshop: Supplier Portal later this year, so this has been on my mind a lot recently. This post grew out of preparation for that event,  specifically the question of how to explain UI Integration Cards to developers and architects who are new to the topic but need to make real implementation decisions fast.

The question teams consistently hit early is not what cards are, but which development path to take and when. There are two fundamentally different approaches:

  • Low-code (declarative): Everything lives in manifest.json. No JavaScript controller, no XML view, no build step. The framework handles rendering, theming, accessibility, and responsiveness. This covers eight of the nine card types and the vast majority of supplier portal use cases.
  • Pro-code (Component card): A full SAPUI5 component embedded in a card frame. Maximum flexibility, but you give up automatic theming, the Admin Console configuration panel, and declarative data binding and you take on full responsibility for Fiori compliance and the code maintenance.

Choosing the wrong path creates rework. This post maps both paths with supplier portal context throughout, then gives you a decision framework and highlights the manifest.json patterns, especially Work Zone context bindings and conditional expressions, that are rarely documented in one place.

All code examples are grounded in the official SAP UI5 Card Explorer.

The manifest.json Skeleton — Quick Anatomy

Every card, regardless of type or complexity, uses the same three-namespace structure: sap.app (card identity and metadata), sap.ui (UI5 technology declaration), and sap.card (type and content). The non-negotiable rules: sap.app/type must be "card" (not "application"), sap.app/id must be globally unique across your BTP tenant (use reverse-domain notation), and sap.card/type is the only always-required property within sap.card. For the full schema reference, see the Card Manifest Reference.

{
  "_version": "1.15.0",
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.supplier.cards.my-card",
    "type": "card",
    "applicationVersion": { "version": "1.0.0" }
  },
  "sap.ui": { "technology": "UI5" },
  "sap.card": { "type": "List" }
}

Everything else, such as header, data source, content layout, parameters, destinations is added inside sap.card.

Card Types at a Glance

Eight types are declarative (low-code). One (Component) is the pro-code escape hatch. For the full type documentation and live examples, browse the SAP UI5 Card Explorer directly.

Type Available In Best For

ListSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Orders, alerts, notifications, item feeds
TableSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Inventory tables, reports, structured comparisons
ObjectSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Supplier profiles, order details, record mastercards
TimelineSAPUI5 onlyOnboarding milestones, approval histories, activity logs
AnalyticalSAPUI5 onlyKPI tiles, spend dashboards, bar/donut/line charts
CalendarSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Appointment scheduling, event streams
AdaptiveCardSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Microsoft Adaptive Cards spec content
WebPageSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Embedded web page / iFrame
ComponentSAPUI5 + OpenUI5Full SAPUI5 component — pro-code only

Supplier Portal Use Cases - Card Type Mapping

Before choosing a card type, map your use case to the right type. The table below covers the most common supplier portal scenarios:

Supplier Portal Use Case Card Type Typical Data Source Key manifest.json Pattern

Open purchase orders feedListConditional highlight expression on order amount
Delivery alerts & quality notificationsListhighlight: Error/Warning/Success driven by status field
Invoice status overviewTableOne column per field; "identifier": true on invoice ID
Supplier master data / company profileObjectWork Zone context binding for auto-personalization
Spend KPIs & budget consumptionAnalyticalNumeric header + StackedColumn chart
Delivery performance trendAnalyticalLine or bar chart with trend indicator in header
Onboarding milestone trackerTimelinePer-item icon expression on task status field
Approval history logTimelineChronological task events with dateTime binding
Upcoming supplier calls & meetingsCalendarAppointment template with start/end ISO binding
Custom multi-tab scorecard or map viewComponentFull SAPUI5 component — pro-code path required

Path 1 — Low-Code: Manifest-Only Development

The low-code path covers all eight declarative types. You configure everything, such as data source, layout, interactions inside manifest.json. The framework handles rendering, theming, accessibility, and responsiveness.

For full manifest examples and interactive live previews of each type, the SAP UI5 Card Explorer is the authoritative reference. The four supplier portal scenarios below call out the manifest.json patterns worth understanding before you start: things the documentation covers individually but rarely connects together.

List Card - Open Orders & Alerts

→ Card Explorer: List Card

The List Card is the workhorse for feed-style data: open purchase orders, delivery alerts, quality notifications. Two patterns to know:

  • Binding expressions on highlight, icon, and info fields drive conditional UX entirely declaratively, no controller needed. Syntax: {= ${Amount} > 100000 ? 'Warning' : 'Success'}. The {= ... } expression form works anywhere a string value is expected in the manifest.
  • Configurable parameters ({{parameters.maxItems}}) let portal admins adjust list length in the Admin Console without touching the manifest, making the same card reusable across multiple portal pages with different display needs. Always add withCredentials: true to data.request so the app router forwards the user's Work Zone session to the backend.

Object Card - Supplier Profile

→ Card Explorer: Object Card · Object Card in Focus - SAP Community, Jul 2026

The Object Card renders a single business record as grouped label/value pairs. It is the natural fit for a supplier's master data view. The key pattern: wire a parameter like supplierId to {context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value} (see the Work Zone Context Bindings section below) so the card auto-loads the current user's profile on every page load without any server-side identity resolution logic.

Analytical Card - KPI Dashboard & Spend Charts

→ Card Explorer: Analytical Card

The Analytical Card pairs a "type": "Numeric" header, such as KPI figure, unit, trend indicator, and up to two side indicators with a chart body (StackedColumn, bar, Donut, Line). Use it for spend dashboards, delivery performance KPIs, or quality rate trends on the supplier homepage. Start with inline data.json for a static prototype, then swap in a data.request block to pull from a live OData or REST endpoint. Requires full SAPUI5.

Timeline Card - Onboarding Progress

→ Card Explorer: Timeline Card

The Timeline Card renders ordered, time-stamped events. It is the right choice for supplier onboarding milestone trackers or approval histories. Combine with a {{parameters.currentUser}} context binding (see below) to scope the timeline to the logged-in supplier's workflow instances. Binding expressions work on icon.src too: {= ${status} === 'COMPLETED' ? 'sap-icon://accept' : 'sap-icon://pending'} drives per-item icons dynamically with no controller.

Connecting Cards to SAP BTP Destinations

When a card runs inside SAP Build Work Zone, all backend calls are proxied through the application router. You cannot use absolute backend URLs, but you must declare named destinations and reference them as {{destinations.myDestination}}.

The BTP destination (BTP Cockpit → Connectivity → Destinations) must include these additional properties:

Property Required Value Why

HTML5.DynamicDestinationtrueMandatory. Allows the app router to resolve the destination dynamically at runtime. Without it, card requests return 404 or fail silently.
WebIDEEnabledtrueRequired for SAP Business Application Studio tooling to detect the destination.
WebIDEUsageodata_genUse odata_abap for ABAP systems; SuccessFactorsExtensionCard for SuccessFactors.

Declare the destination in the manifest under configuration.destinations:

{
  "sap.card": {
    "configuration": {
      "destinations": {
        "s4hana": {
          "name": "MY_S4H_DESTINATION",
          "defaultUrl": "/sap/opu/odata/sap/",
          "label": "S/4HANA Backend"
        }
      }
    },
    "data": {
      "request": {
        "url": "{{destinations.s4hana}}/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner",
        "parameters": { "$format": "json", "$top": "10" },
        "withCredentials": true
      },
      "path": "/d/results"
    }
  }
}

The name property maps the manifest's logical alias (s4hana) to the physical BTP destination name. This indirection means you can change the target system without editing the manifest. This is very useful when promoting cards across landscapes.

Work Zone Context Bindings 

This is one of the most practically useful patterns in the card framework, and one of the least documented in one place. Work Zone injects a set of context variables at runtime that you can bind directly to card parameters to enable personalized, identity-aware cards with zero server-side user resolution logic.

Here is an example using the Context Bindings as a data. 

"configuration": {
  "parameters": {
    "currentUserId": {
      "value": "{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    },
    "tenantHost": {
      "value": "{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/webHost/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    },
    "sfUserId": {
      "value": "{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/id/value}",
      "type": "string",
      "visible": false
    }
  }
}

Once declared, reference them anywhere in the manifest with {{parameters.currentUserId}} — including inside data.request.url, $filter query parameters, or request headers.

Complete Context Variable Reference

Context Variable Description Availability

{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}Logged-in user's UUID in Work ZoneWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/name/value}Logged-in user's display nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/email/value}Logged-in user's email addressWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/firstName/value}User's first nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentUser/lastName/value}User's last nameWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/id/value}Work Zone company/tenant IDWZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.workzone/currentCompany/webHost/value}Tenant web host (for constructing URLs)WZ Standard & Advanced
{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/id/value}SAP SuccessFactors user IDSuccessFactors Work Zone
{context>sap.successfactors/currentUser/name/value}SAP SuccessFactors display nameSuccessFactors Work Zone

Practical use cases for supplier portals:

  • Personalized data fetch: use currentUser/id to filter an OData query to the current supplier's records.
  • Dynamic URL construction: use currentCompany/webHost to build tenant-specific deep links in navigation actions.
  • SuccessFactors cross-scenario: if your supplier portal also hosts HR self-service cards, sap.successfactors/currentUser/id lets you target SF OData endpoints without a separate identity resolution call.

Path 2 — Pro-Code: Component Cards

The Component card type loads a full SAPUI5 component. Essentially it is a mini-application embedded in a card frame. Choose this path only when:

  • Your layout cannot be expressed by any of the eight declarative types (e.g., a custom multi-tab view, a map widget, a D3 chart).
  • You need complex client-side business logic (multi-step form validation, dynamic data dependencies between fields).
  • You are wrapping an existing SAPUI5 application fragment as a card.

The manifest for a Component card delegates rendering to SAPUI5:

{
  "_version": "1.15.0",
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.supplier.cards.custom-scorecard",
    "type": "card",
    "applicationVersion": { "version": "1.0.0" }
  },
  "sap.card": {
    "type": "Component",
    "header": {
      "title": "Supplier Scorecard",
      "subTitle": "Custom performance view"
    }
  },
  "sap.ui5": {
    "rootView": {
      "viewName": "com.company.supplier.cards.custom-scorecard.view.Main",
      "type": "XML",
      "async": true
    },
    "dependencies": {
      "minUI5Version": "1.90.0",
      "libs": {
        "sap.ui.core":   {},
        "sap.m":         {},
        "sap.ui.layout": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

The corresponding project structure adds a full SAPUI5 component alongside the manifest:

my-component-card/
├── manifest.json
├── Component.js            ← SAPUI5 UIComponent
├── view/
│   └── Main.view.xml       ← XML view
├── controller/
│   └── Main.controller.js
└── i18n/
    └── i18n.properties

The architectural cost to factor in: Component cards require you to manually implement SAP Fiori design guidelines. The automatic theming, accessibility guarantees, and Admin Console configuration panel that declarative cards provide for free become your responsibility. This also means that when SAP updates Work Zone's design system or theming tokens, your Component card will not automatically pick up the changes. 

Decision Framework: Which Path Should You Choose?

Use these questions to reach the right decision before writing any code:

Question If YES → Recommendation

Does your data fit a list, table, object, chart, or timeline pattern?Low-CodeUse the corresponding declarative type
Do you need the card to be configurable by portal admins (no code)?Low-CodeUse configuration.parameters
Is the card connecting to a single BTP destination OData/REST endpoint?Low-CodeDeclarative data.request handles this
Do you need per-user personalization?Low-CodeUse Work Zone context bindings
Does your layout require multiple tabs, a wizard, or a custom chart library?Pro-CodeUse Component card
Do you need complex client-side validation or multi-step logic?Pro-CodeUse Component card
Will non-developers maintain or reconfigure the card post-deployment?Low-CodeDeclarative cards have a built-in admin UI
Are you wrapping an existing SAPUI5 app fragment?Pro-CodeComponent card is the right vessel

If the answer to most questions points to Low-Code but one layout requirement pushes toward Pro-Code, reconsider the layout requirement first. A different declarative type or a grouped Object card often solves what initially seems to need a custom component.

Project Structure and Tooling

A complete low-code card project in SAP Business Application Studio:

my-card-project/
├── manifest.json             ← Card definition (only required file)
├── i18n/
│   ├── i18n.properties       ← Default translations
│   └── i18n_de.properties    ← German translations
├── dt/
│   └── configuration.js      ← Design-time editor 
└── data/
    └── sample-data.json      ← Static data for BAS preview

Reference i18n keys anywhere in the manifest with double-brace syntax (same as parameters):

{
  "sap.app": {
    "id": "com.company.cards.orders",
    "type": "card",
    "i18n": "i18n/i18n.properties"
  },
  "sap.card": {
    "header": {
      "title": "{{CARD_TITLE}}",
      "subTitle": "{{CARD_SUBTITLE}}"
    }
  }
}
# i18n/i18n.properties
CARD_TITLE=Open Purchase Orders
CARD_SUBTITLE=Requires your attention

Summary

The key takeaways for architects designing content on SAP Build Work Zone for supplier portal scenarios:

  • Default to declarative. List, Table, Object, Analytical, and Timeline cards cover the standard supplier portal scenarios. The framework's rendering, theming, and Admin Console integration are worth preserving.
  • Use Work Zone context bindings ({context>sap.workzone/currentUser/id/value}) to build personalized, identity-aware cards without server-side user resolution logic. This pattern is underused and more powerful than it looks.
  • Use binding expressions ({= ${field} > threshold ? 'Warning' : 'Success'}) for conditional UX — colours, icons, labels — without needing a controller.
  • Get the BTP destination right first. HTML5.DynamicDestination: true is not optional, and the July 2025 alias change in Standard Edition catches teams that haven't updated.
  • Reserve Component for genuine outliers — complex layouts or logic that the declarative model cannot express — and factor in the Admin Console governance cost before committing.

The full reference for all card types, manifest properties, and live examples is available in the SAP UI5 Card Explorer.

References

SAP UI5 Card Explorer

  • Card Explorer (all types, live examples)
  • Card Manifest Reference
  • Design-Time Configuration API

SAP Help Portal

Who are you, what do you like to do, what is important to you?

I was born in Rome, and ever since I was a child, I dreamt of becoming a programmer because of my love for computers. I started my career many years ago developing in ABAP, and it's still my first love, I've never really put it down. Ever since my early years in the SAP Community, I have always found great inspiration in the SAP Mentors. When I first joined the SAP Community, my goal was to find solutions to the technical problems I faced in my programming career. To get the most out of the SAP Community, I believe it's truly beneficial to participate in initiatives such as Inside Track events, CodeJam, and similar activities. entry.title: Bridging OpenUI5 and UI5 Web Components
entry.content:
OpenUI5 and UI5 Web Components use different programming models. OpenUI5 is based on controls, metadata, aggregations, events, lifecycle, and data binding, while UI5 Web Components are based on web standards and expose functionality through properties, attributes, slots, and custom events.

This difference creates a technical challenge when integrating the UI5 Web Components Table (ui5-table) into OpenUI5. Rendering a <ui5-table> element in the DOM alone does not make it an OpenUI5 control or integrate it with OpenUI5 concepts such as aggregations, lifecycle, and data binding.

The objective is to integrate the Table into OpenUI5 in a way that aligns with the OpenUI5 programming model. To achieve this, ui5-tooling-modules can generate OpenUI5 wrappers for UI5 Web Components based on their metadata. These generated wrappers can then serve as the basis for a custom wrapper layer that provides the required integration with OpenUI5 control concepts.

 

First Attempt: Direct Web Component Usage

The direct approach uses a minimal setup without generated wrapper controls or an additional integration layer.  A custom OpenUI5 control extends sap.ui.core.Control, and its renderer writes the Web Component tags directly into the DOM.

The setup uses ui5-tooling-modules-middleware to make the Web Component packages available.  Both <ui5-button> and <ui5-table> are rendered using the OpenUI5 render manager. For the button, the rendered element is also queried in onAfterRendering, and its click event is forwarded to an OpenUI5 press event.

The elements are rendered into the DOM without errors, but they are not initialized as UI5 Web Components. The button appears as plain clickable text, and the table does not display its expected structure or behavior.

The missing step is the explicit requirement of the corresponding Web Component module. Making the package available through the middleware does not register the individual component. For example, the Button module needs to be required separately:

sap.ui.define([
    "@ui5/webcomponents/dist/Button"
], function (Button) {
    // ...
});

Without this module requirement, the browser only sees the custom HTML tag and the Web Component is not initialized.

This shows that rendering the Web Component tag is not sufficient for integration with OpenUI5. The component also needs to be connected to the OpenUI5 control model and lifecycle. This leads to the wrapper-based approach.

 

Building the Wrapper

An OpenUI5 wrapper provides the integration layer between the two programming models. OpenUI5 handles the control structure, lifecycle, metadata, and data binding, while the UI5 Web Component handles its own rendering. Web Component properties, slots, and custom events are mapped to the corresponding OpenUI5 control concepts.

The wrapper consists of two layers. The first layer is the generated wrapper, which ui5-tooling-modules generates from the Web Component metadata. It provides the OpenUI5 control definition, including properties, aggregations, and events. Web Component slots are mapped to OpenUI5 aggregations during this process. The generated files are recreated during the generation process and are therefore kept separate from project-specific code.

The second layer contains the custom wrappers used by the application. For the Table integration, this includes wrappers for the Table, rows, cells, header rows, and header cells. Each custom wrapper extends its corresponding generated wrapper.

The wrapper structure is:

 

The custom Table wrapper follows a minimal pattern:

 

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/m/gen/ui5/webcomponents/dist/Table"
], function (WebCTable) {
    "use strict";

    return WebCTable.extend("sap.m.wct.TableCustomWrapper", {
        metadata: {
            library: "sap.m",
            tag: WebCTable.getMetadata().getTag()
        }
    });
});

Here, WebCTable is the generated OpenUI5 wrapper, and TableCustomWrapper extends it. The library metadata places the custom control in the sap.m library, while tag connects it to the corresponding UI5 Web Component. The custom wrapper does not implement its own Table renderer because the generated wrapper already provides the required mapping.

An early version of the custom wrapper redefined the headerRow and rows aggregations. This caused the Table to fail during rendering, with the browser console showing:

 

Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '0')

The generated wrapper already contained these aggregations based on the Web Component metadata and slot definitions. Redefining them in the custom wrapper created conflicting metadata. Removing the duplicate definitions resolved the error and kept the custom wrapper limited to the metadata it actually needs.

 

Project Configuration

The wrapper generation uses ui5-tooling-modules to process the UI5 Web Components packages and generate the corresponding OpenUI5 wrappers from their metadata.

For the UI libraries in the OpenUI5 repository, customTasks cannot be used for the build, so the wrappers need to be generated upfront and integrated into the project sources. This is why the project uses a separate generation script with the UI5 CLI.

The relevant Web Component packages are provided to ui5-tooling-modules, while the entryPoints property defines the components required by the project:

entryPoints:
  - "@ui5/webcomponents/dist/Table.js"
  - "@ui5/webcomponents/dist/TableRow.js"
  - "@ui5/webcomponents/dist/TableCell.js"
  - "@ui5/webcomponents/dist/TableHeaderRow.js"
  - "@ui5/webcomponents/dist/TableHeaderCell.js"

For the Table integration, the entry points include the Table itself together with its row, cell, and header components. During the generation step, the ui5-tooling-modules-task processes the entryPoints configuration to generate the corresponding wrapper controls.

The generation is handled by three npm scripts:

"scripts": {
    "build-webcomponents": "ui5 build --dest ./src/sap/m --output-style flat --config ui5-build.yaml --exclude-task * --include-task ui5-tooling-modules-task",
    "clean-webcomponents": "node -e \"const fsx = require('fs-extra'); fsx.emptyDirSync('src/sap/m/gen'); fsx.emptyDirSync('src/sap/m/thirdparty');\"",
    "generate-webcomponents": "npm run clean-webcomponents && npm run build-webcomponents"
}

generate-webcomponents first removes the previous generated output and then runs the UI5 CLI build with the ui5-tooling-modules-task enabled. This makes the wrapper generation repeatable and integrates the generated controls into the project sources.

Running:

npm run generate-webcomponents

generates the wrapper controls under:

src/sap/m/gen/ui5/webcomponents/dist/

 

 

The generated controls remain separate from the custom wrappers under src/sap/m/wct/. This allows the generated layer to be recreated without overwriting project-specific code.

For a detailed configuration example, see the ui5-build.yaml file for the sap.f library in the OpenUI5 repository.

 

Data Binding with the Wrapped Table

The wrapped Table supports standard OpenUI5 aggregation binding with both a local JSONModel and an ODataModel connected to the Northwind OData V2 service.

The local example uses a dataset with three rows and three columns:

const data = {
    rows: [
        { col1: "Laptop",   col2: 12500, col3: "Germany" },
        { col1: "Monitor",  col2: 8400,  col3: "France" },
        { col1: "Keyboard", col2: 3200,  col3: "UK" }
    ],
    columns: [
        { label: "Product" },
        { label: "Revenue" },
        { label: "Region" }
    ]
};

const model = new JSONModel(data);
oTable.setModel(model);

The row aggregation is bound to the model through standard OpenUI5 aggregation binding. A row template defines how one model entry maps to a TableRow and its TableCell controls. OpenUI5 creates the corresponding rows and resolves the binding expressions for each cell.

Column definitions are handled separately through a factory function for the header cells. The row data and header structure therefore remain within the OpenUI5 control and binding model without direct DOM manipulation. The Table renders the local data correctly in the Snippix test environment. 

The OData example uses an ODataModel connected to the Northwind OData V2 service:

const url = "/databinding/proxy/https://services.odata.org/V2/Northwind/...";

const oDataModel = new ODataModel(url, {
    json: true,
    useBatch: false
});

oTable.setModel(oDataModel);

A separate JSONModel provides the column definitions:

const columnsData = {
    columns: [
        { label: "Product Name" },
        { label: "Product Sales" },
        { label: "Category" }
    ]
};

const columnModel = new JSONModel(columnsData);
oTable.setModel(columnModel, "columns");

The row aggregation is bound to the OData entity set, with the row template mapping its cells to properties returned by the service. Multiple product rows are displayed correctly in the Table. The proxy path is specific to the test environment and is used to avoid cross-origin restrictions when accessing the external service; it is not part of the wrapper itself.

 

 

Both data sources use the same OpenUI5 aggregation-binding mechanism. OpenUI5 handles aggregation binding, child-control creation, model updates, and propagation of bound values. The wrapper does not require a custom bindRows() helper or additional binding logic.

The wrapped Table can therefore be used through the standard OpenUI5 model and aggregation-binding concepts, while the UI5 Web Component remains behind the wrapper layer.

 

Looking Ahead

The wrapper pattern is not specific to the Table. The same generated-wrapper and custom-wrapper approach can also be applied to other UI5 Web Components, such as inputs, dialogs, and cards.

The generated wrapper provides the basic mapping from the Web Component metadata, while the custom wrapper provides an extension point for project-specific functionality and OpenUI5-specific requirements.

For the Table, further extensions can include additional features and broader automated test coverage to evaluate the integration more extensively.

 

Conclusion

This implementation integrates a UI5 Web Component into OpenUI5 while aligning it with the OpenUI5 control model.

The UI5 Web Components Table can be exposed through OpenUI5 properties and aggregations and used with standard aggregation binding for both JSONModel and ODataModel. OpenUI5 continues to handle the control structure and data binding, while the UI5 Web Component remains responsible for rendering its UI.

The implementation is not a drop-in replacement for native OpenUI5 controls and requires further work before it can be considered production-ready.  However, the prototype shows that generated and custom wrappers provide the integration needed to use UI5 Web Components within the OpenUI5 programming model.

entry.title: Smart Report - Example with VA05N (List of Sales Orders)
entry.content:
I’ve designed numerous processes, reports, and APIs. However, traditional development often ties solutions tightly to specific user requirements, which limits flexibility. My goal has always been to build open, configurable solutions where users can adjust behavior through settings rather than code changes.

A recurring challenge remains: How do we design systems that give users maximum flexibility in how they query and retrieve information from the backend?

With the emergence of LLMs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), this challenge is becoming easier to solve. By exposing SAP backend services through MCP, users can interact with SAP data using natural language, and the LLM can generate meaningful responses dynamically.

To explore this idea further, I experimented with enabling LLM‑based querying on report data — essentially creating a Smart Report concept. For testing, I used the SAP VA05N report, surfaced its data through a SAPUI5 application, and added intelligent features powered by LLMs. This approach demonstrates how traditional SAP reports can evolve into flexible, conversational, and insight‑driven tools.

The Architecture         :

The Output     :

SAP Back-end Designed :

Designed and implemented the ZREPORT_RAG database table to persist user RAG session details, enabling comprehensive session logging and traceability. The solution also includes logic to identify and remove any existing active session before creating a new one, ensuring data consistency and preventing duplicate or stale session records.

 

Developed the class ZCL_REPORT_CORE to centralize the core processing logic for the application, including the primary methods GET_VA05N_DATA, CREATE_RAG, and GET_RAG. To retrieve the executed report output efficiently, the implementation leverages the standard SAP class CL_SALV_BS_RUNTIME_INFO, specifically its GET_DATA_REF method, enabling seamless access to ALV report data post‑execution. Additional handling was incorporated to manage data extraction, transformation, and preparation for downstream RAG generation within the application workflow.

Subsequently, an OData service ZREPORTS was developed using the SEGW transaction. Two entities were modeled: raginfo, backed by the ZREPORT_RAG table, and va05n, based on the SVBMTV_TRVOG structure.

The corresponding entity methods—RAGINFOSET_CREATE_ENTITY, RAGINFOSET_GET_ENTITY, and VA05NSET_GET_ENTITYSET—were redefined to integrate the core logic from ZCL_REPORT_CORE, invoking CREATE_RAG, GET_RAG, and GET_VA05N_DATA respectively. This enabled the creation and retrieval of RAG session logs as well as the delivery of VA05N report data to the SAPUI5 application.

Ollama

Deployed the Ollama instance inside a Docker container to ensure a clean, reproducible, and easily maintainable environment for local model experimentation.

After the deployment, installed a set of models tailored for coding assistance, general reasoning, and text‑embedding workflows:

  • qwen2.5-coder:latest — optimized for code generation, debugging, and developer‑focused tasks.
  • llama3.1:latest — a versatile general‑purpose model suitable for reasoning, drafting, and broader language tasks.
  • nomic-embed-text:latest — used for generating high‑quality text embeddings, ideal for semantic search, RAG pipelines, and similarity scoring.

Together, these models provide a balanced setup for development: strong coding support, reliable general LLM capabilities, and efficient embedding generation for retrieval‑augmented applications.

Report Analysis Api:

 

Developed a middleware api with following services:

/api/v1/report/session :

Used to store report data—both records and column definitions—into the DuckDB instance. DuckDB’s columnar storage and fast analytical capabilities make this endpoint ideal for capturing structured data that will later be queried, embedded, or analyzed using Ollama models.

/api/v1/report/session/all :

Fetches all currently available report sessions along with their associated metadata. This allows the system to quickly list active datasets stored in DuckDB.

/api/v1/report/session/{session_id} :

Deletes a specific session using its unique session ID. Removing outdated or unnecessary sessions helps maintain a clean DuckDB environment and ensures that Ollama models operate only on relevant datasets during query generation or embedding workflows.

/api/v1/report/qa :

Processes a query against a selected session and returns a formatted, model‑generated response. This endpoint typically uses DuckDB to retrieve the relevant data and then leverages Ollama models—such as qwen2.5‑coder, llama3.1, or nomic‑embed‑text—to perform reasoning, generate answers, or produce embeddings for RAG‑style responses.

/api/v1/report/getForecast :

Generates forward‑looking time‑series predictions by retrieving historical date–value data based on passing into formated date and value details, and applying high‑performance forecasting models from the StatsForecast Python library. Once the endpoint extracts and prepares the dataset, it leverages AutoARIMA to automatically identify the optimal ARIMA configuration based on temporal patterns, and AutoETS to model trend and seasonality using exponential smoothing. These complementary models allow the system to produce accurate forecasts for the specified horizon, while DuckDB ensures fast analytical retrieval and preprocessing. The endpoint can also optionally pair the numerical output with an Ollama model to provide narrative explanations or contextual insights, creating a lightweight yet powerful forecasting workflow suitable for analytical reporting and decision support.

The Front-end:

Developed a SAPUI5 application by using the OData backend service and Report Analysis Middleware API.

On load, RAGINFOSET_GET_ENTITY call to fetch latest generated user specific session details from SAP system and store into model variable.

Then on load of view, VA05NSET_GET_ENTITYSET service call to fetch all VA05N report data and display into smart table as below :

 

 

The table toolbar provides two key options

  1. Activate Smart Report and
  2. Chat

that work together to enable AI‑driven analysis. When the user selects Activate Smart Report, the current table view, including all visible fields, is sent to DuckDB by triggering the /api/v1/report/session endpoint; before creating this new session, the system deletes any previously stored session for that user to prevent stale or outdated data from influencing query generation, ensure the AI always works with the latest table snapshot, and maintain a clean one‑session‑per‑user workflow. Once the new session is successfully stored in DuckDB, the Chat option becomes active, allowing the user to ask questions against the freshly loaded dataset and receive model‑generated responses based on the most current information.

The system shows the user’s request in the chat area in a clean, easy‑to‑read format, just like a normal messaging app :

 

Details available into back-end system (VA05N T-Code 😞

 

Added a few more features related to the tabular data, as shown in the screen below.

 

 

At the top of any table‑based response, users can switch how the data is shown—either as a table or as an analytics view. For analytics, they can choose Bar, Line, Area, or Pie charts to better understand the information. These options are available only when the response contains tabular data.

Added another feature specifically for Date‑and‑Value datasets that allows users to generate forecasts or time‑series projections for up to 10 future periods.

For example, in the scenario below, the system calculates the total net value based on the “created‑on” dates and then applies a forecast to generate the next five future periods.

All program and logic details are available into :

https://github.com/ipravir/Smart-Report

This solution is built on an SAP EHP8 system and uses a local Ollama model, which is perfectly suitable for development, testing, and proving the overall concept. Moving to the SAP AI Core LLM service in the future can make responses faster, improve performance under heavy workloads, and provide better reliability as the application grows. The project also updates SAP ABAP syntax based on the system and kernel version, using newer and more efficient language features to improve runtime performance and maintainability.

Happy Learning 😀

Praveer

#SAP #SAPUI5 #ABAP #GenerativeAI #RAG #Ollama #DuckDB #Python #TimeSeriesForecasting #BusinessIntelligence #EnterpriseAI #SAPInnovation

entry.title: Implementing Internationalization in SAP CAP: Multi-Language Support Using i18n Properties
entry.content:
Introduction

Enterprise applications rarely serve users from a single country. A Fiori app built in Bengaluru may well be used by someone in Paris or Frankfurt, and showing them English column headers everywhere isn't a great experience.

Internationalization (i18n) solves this. Instead of hardcoding texts such as Name, City, or General Information directly in CDS annotations, we externalize them into language-specific properties files. At runtime, the application loads the appropriate language-specific texts, allowing the UI to change languages without modifying the underlying application logic.

In this blog, I'll build a small CAP application with a Fiori Elements UI and demonstrate English and French translations using i18n properties files. The same approach can be extended to additional languages such as German, Hindi, and Kannada.

What actually gets translated

One thing confused me when I first set this up, so let me get it out of the way early: there are two separate i18n layers in a CAP + Fiori Elements project, and they sit in different folders.

The first is the CAP layer, a folder named _i18n at the project root. This is what translates the labels in your CDS annotations: field labels, facet headers, that kind of thing. The CAP layer is responsible for resolving i18n keys used in CDS annotations, such as field labels and facet titles, before the corresponding OData metadata is consumed by the Fiori Elements application.

The second is the UI5 layer, the i18n folder inside webapp. This handles the app title, description, and any texts you reference directly from your UI5 views or controllers. It's resolved in the browser by the standard UI5 resource model.
