entry.title: SAP Developer tools are available on Open VSX Registry
entry.content:
SAP Developer Tools Are Now on Open VSX Registry!

 

Why That Matters

Developers don’t all work in the same editor. Some live in Visual Studio Code or VS Code. Some use Eclipse Theia-based environments in the cloud. And a growing number run AI-native editors where VS Code compatibility is the baseline — but the Microsoft Marketplace is not.

This isn’t a niche edge case. The VS Code-compatible editor ecosystem has expanded significantly, and Microsoft’s extension marketplace is not accessible from most of them. For SAP developers working in those environments, that has historically meant missing out on the tooling they need to build SAP applications effectively.

We hope that this changes with SAP’s publication on Open VSX (open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE).

What Is Open VSX Registry?

Open VSX is a vendor-neutral extension registry operated by the Eclipse Foundation. It is the standard distribution channel for VS Code extensions in any editor that does not have direct access to the Microsoft Marketplace — which covers a wide and growing set of environments used by professional developers today.

 

Where the Microsoft Marketplace is tied to the Microsoft ecosystem, Open VSX is open infrastructure. Any VS Code-compatible editor can consume it. Any publisher can list extensions without vendor agreements. It is how the broader editor ecosystem accesses the extension tooling it needs.

SAP’s Developer Strategy: Choice Without Compromise

SAP’s position is straightforward: developers should be able to work in the environment that makes them most productive. The SAP tooling needed to build cloud applications, Fiori UIs, and mobile solutions should follow them there — not require them to switch editors.

 

Publishing on Open VSX is how SAP delivers on that. It ensures that SAP’s developer extensions are available wherever VS Code-compatible editors are used, without requiring developers to compromise on their setup.

This is the direct continuation of the work announced in this VS Code extensions blog.

What’s Published Under the SAPSE Namespace

The following eight extensions are available today at open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE:

SAP CDS Language Support

Language support for SAP Core Data Services delivers syntax highlighting, Language Server Protocol integration, real-time diagnostics, and formatting for .cds files. The foundational extension for SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) development — if you’re building CAP services, this is where you start.

Core Data Services Graphical Modeler

CDS Graphical Modeler allows the developer to model CDS files in SAP Cloud Application Programming model development projects and enables increased productivity in designing CDS model via the graphical editor. Both CAP (.cds) and ABAP CDS (.csn) files can be edited.

SAP Fiori Tools — Extension Pack

A bundled pack that installs the full SAP Fiori development toolchain in one step. The recommended starting point for any Fiori Elements or SAPUI5 project.

SAP Fiori Tools — Application Modeler

A visual representation of a Fiori application’s page structure, navigation targets, and service entities. The Page Map view lets you add navigation, manage pages, and modify application structure directly — no manual configuration file editing required.

SAP Fiori Tools — XML Annotation Language Server

Authoring support for OData annotations — the metadata layer that drives how Fiori Elements applications render and behave. Provides code completion, micro-snippets, i18n support, and real-time diagnostics as you write annotation files.

SAP Fiori Tools — Service Modeler

A combined view of an OData service and its associated annotations helping to understand a service’s structure and annotation coverage without parsing raw metadata — particularly when connecting Fiori applications to SAP backend systems.

SAP Fiori Tools — Guided Development

In-editor access to how-to guides and step-by-step tutorials for implementing Fiori Elements features. Contextual guidance surfaces during development, so the relevant SAP documentation is available without leaving the editor.

Mobile Development Kit Editor

Visual development tools for the mobile development kit, SAP's platform for building enterprise-grade cross-platform mobile applications with offline capabilities, OData backend synchronization, and deployment across iOS and Android. The end-to-end development capabilities includes visual editing, debugging support, and code snippets, enabling developers to build, debug, and maintain mobile applications directly within the IDE.

Getting Started

If you’re working in a Visual Studio Code-compatible editor, search for SAPSE in your extension marketplace — or navigate directly to open-vsx.org/namespace/SAPSE. 

While Visual Studio Code users can continue using the Microsoft Marketplace/SAP SE as before. Open VSX serves developers who work in other growing ecosystem of editors built on VS Code’s foundations.

The extensions are the same. The tooling is the same. The only difference is that more developers can now use it — in the editor they choose.

Follow SAP Application Development on the SAP Community for updates on developer tooling, CAP, Fiori development, and mobile.

entry.title: Showcasing News and Highlights in SAPUI5 using the sap.m.SlideTile Control
entry.content:
Hello everyone,

In this blog post I'm going to explain the SlideTile control in SAPUI5 in a simple way, with the steps I followed while trying it out.

Overview

In simple words, SlideTile is a control that shows several tiles one after another in the sam space, switching between them automatically after a few seconds. Instead of placing four or five tiles side by side on a page, we place them inside one SlideTile, and it rotates through them.

For example, on a Fiori launchpad home page or a dashboard we may want to show "latest news", "announcements" or "featured apps". If we show each of these as a separate tile, the page quickly becomes crowded. With SlideTile, all of them share a single tile slot, and the user can still see each one in turn.

So here I created a small project where I took two news-style tiles and showed them in two SlideTile controls, one with the default timing and one with custom timing, and handled the click on each tile.

Why I used SlideTile instead of building it myself

At first I thought of building this rotation on my own using a timer in the controller, swapping the tile content and adding some CSS for the animation. But then I realized SAPUI5 already provides a standard control for this, so I did not have to write the timer, the transition animation or the navigation indicator myself. Since it is a standard Fiori control, it also looks and behaves like the tiles in other Fiori apps, without any extra styling.

Project Structure

The important files are inside the webapp folder: the view, the controller and manifest.json, same as any normal SAPUI5 app.

 
project1/
├── webapp/
│   ├── controller/
│   │   ├── App.controller.js
│   │   └── View1.controller.js
│   ├── css/
│   ├── i18n/
│   ├── images/
│   │   ├── smarthome.jpg
│   │   └── inventory.jpg
│   ├── model/
│   ├── test/
│   ├── view/
│   │   ├── App.view.xml
│   │   └── View1.view.xml
│   ├── Component.js
│   ├── index.html
│   └── manifest.json
├── package.json
└── README.md

SlideTile is only a container. The actual content comes from the tiles we put inside it

  • SlideTile rotates its child tiles one after another.
  • GenericTile is one slide. It holds the background image, the size (frameType) and the press behaviour.
  • TileContent holds the footer text of the tile.
  • NewsContent holds the headline (contentText) and the small sub heading (subheader).

Step 1: Create the view (View1.view.xml)

<mvc:View controllerName="project1.controller.View1"
	xmlns="sap.m"
	xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc"
	xmlns:l="sap.ui.layout">
	<l:VerticalLayout>

		<!-- SlideTile 1: default timing -->
		<SlideTile class="sapUiTinyMarginBegin sapUiTinyMarginTop">
			<GenericTile
				backgroundImage="images/smarthome.jpg"
				frameType="TwoByOne"
				press=".pressOnTileOne">
				<TileContent footer="August 21, 2016">
					<NewsContent
						contentText="SAP Unveils Powerful New Player Comparison Tool Exclusively on NFL.com"
						subheader="Today, SAP News" />
				</TileContent>
			</GenericTile>
			<GenericTile
				backgroundImage="../images/inventory.jpg"
				frameType="TwoByOne"
				press=".pressOnTileTwo">
				<TileContent footer="August 21, 2016">
					<NewsContent
						contentText="Wind Map: Monitoring Real-Time and Forecasted Wind Conditions across the Globe"
						subheader="Today, SAP News" />
				</TileContent>
			</GenericTile>
		</SlideTile>

		<!-- SlideTile 2: custom timing, second tile in Failed state -->
		<SlideTile class="sapUiTinyMarginBegin sapUiTinyMarginTop"
			transitionTime="250"
			displayTime="2500">
			<GenericTile
				backgroundImage="../images/maintenance.jpg"
				frameType="TwoByOne"
				press=".pressOnTileOne">
				<TileContent footer="August 21, 2016">
					<NewsContent
						contentText="Wind Map: Monitoring Real-Time and Forecasted Wind Conditions across the Globe"
						subheader="Today, SAP News" />
				</TileContent>
			</GenericTile>
			<GenericTile
				backgroundImage="../images/supplychain.jpg"
				frameType="TwoByOne"
				state="Failed">
				<TileContent footer="August 21, 2016">
					<NewsContent
						contentText="SAP Unveils Powerful New Player Comparison Tool Exclusively on NFL.com"
						subheader="Today, SAP News" />
				</TileContent>
			</GenericTile>
		</SlideTile>

	</l:VerticalLayout>
</mvc:View>

A few important points about the view:

  • frameType="TwoByOne" gives the wide tile shape, which suits news and banner-style content. Keep the same frame type on all tiles inside one SlideTile so the size doesn't jump during the transition.
  • displayTime is how long each tile stays visible, in milliseconds. If we don't set it, the default is used (5000 ms). In the second SlideTile I set it to 2500, so it rotates faster.
  • transitionTime is how long the slide animation takes, in milliseconds. The default is 500 ms, and I set 250 in the second SlideTile for a quicker slide.
  • state="Failed" on the second tile of the second SlideTile shows the standard error state of a tile. This is useful when the data behind a tile could not be loaded. I used it only to see how it looks, and it has no press handler, so clicking it does nothing.
  • backgroundImage sets the picture behind the text. The text stays readable because the control adds its own overlay.

Step 2: Handle tile clicks (View1.controller.js)

sap.ui.define([
	"sap/ui/core/mvc/Controller",
	"sap/m/MessageToast"
], function (Controller, MessageToast) {
	"use strict";

	return Controller.extend("project1.controller.View1", {

		pressOnTileOne: function () {
			MessageToast.show("The generic tile one pressed.");
		},

		pressOnTileTwo: function () {
			MessageToast.show("The generic tile two pressed.");
		}
	});
});

Whenever the user clicks a tile, the press event of that GenericTile calls the function we gave in the view. Here I have just shown a MessageToast, but in a real application this is the place where we can navigate to the full news article or open the related app.

Conclusion

So, this is how we can use the SlideTile control in SAPUI5 to show several tiles in the space of one. Instead of filling the page with separate tiles, we can place them inside a SlideTile and let the control rotate through them. We only need to give it the GenericTiles, and the control takes care of the rest: the automatic switching, the slide animation and the page indicator, along with the standard Fiori look, without any extra code. We can adjust the speed with displayTime and transitionTime, show a problem with the state property, and react to clicks with the press event.

This same pattern is not limited to news. We can reuse it for announcements, featured apps or KPI highlights on a dashboard, just by changing the content of the tiles. We can also bind the tiles to a JSON or OData model, so the slides are created from data instead of being written one by one in the view.

What This Is About

SAP Fiori remains the user experience foundation for SAP applications. But in 2026, the way users work with SAP solutions has fundamentally shifted. The same holds for the way developers build them.

Joule Work has emerged as the new UI for AI, becoming the primary engagement layer for business users. Joule Studio is the new AI-first development environment for creating agents, apps, and workflows. And familiar technologies like SAPUI5, SAP Fiori elements, and SAP Build haven't gone away, they've evolved and gained new roles in this landscape.

If you've ever caught yourself wondering:

  • How does SAP Fiori fit into a world where Joule is everywhere?
  • What's the relationship between Joule Work, Joule Studio, and SAP Build?
  • Where do I start or continue my learning journey in 2026?

…then this webinar is for you.

This session is designed for everyone: executives, project managers, UX leads, key users, consultants, and developers alike. Whether you've been following SAP Fiori for years or are just now trying to take first steps, you'll leave with a clear mental map of how the pieces fit together today.

This one-hour webinar is structured around the key layers of the SAP UX landscape:

  • SAP Fiori: The UX Foundation The design system, SAPUI5, SAP Fiori elements, and why they still matter in the age of AI.

entry.title: Export SAPUI5 Table Data to Excel in SAP Fiori: Code Examples and Best Practices
entry.content:
Export SAPUI5 Table Data to Excel in SAP Fiori: A Practical Guide with Code Examples

Introduction

Exporting table data to Microsoft Excel is a common requirement in SAP Fiori applications. Business users often need to download data for reporting, offline analysis, reconciliation, and collaboration.

SAPUI5 provides the sap.ui.export.Spreadsheet API to generate Excel workbooks. Developers can define column headers, data types, file names, and which fields are included in the exported spreadsheet.

This blog explains how to implement Excel export in a freestyle SAPUI5 application using an employee-management example. It also covers exporting selected columns, using readable column headers, and handling common issues.

1. Prerequisites

  • An SAPUI5 freestyle application.
  • A table bound to a JSON model or another supported data source.
  • An export button in the table toolbar.
  • The sap.ui.export library available in the SAPUI5 runtime.

For API details and supported export settings, refer to the SAPUI5 Demo Kit.

2. Understand the export approach

The basic process consists of four steps:

  1. Retrieve the table data from the model.
  2. Define the Excel columns using readable labels and model property names.
  3. Configure the spreadsheet and file name.
  4. Generate the workbook and download the .xlsx file.

The column label becomes the Excel header, while property identifies the source field in each row.

3. Create a sample table in the XML view

This example uses an employee table with Employee ID, Employee Name, and Department columns.

<mvc:View
    controllerName="demo.controller.Employee"
    xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc"
    xmlns="sap.m">
    <Page title="Employee Overview">
        <content>
            <Table id="employeeTable" items="{/Employees}">
                <headerToolbar>
                    <OverflowToolbar>
                        <Title text="Employee List" />
                        <ToolbarSpacer />
                        <Button
                            text="Export to Excel"
                            icon="sap-icon://excel-attachment"
                            press=".onExportExcel" />
                    </OverflowToolbar>
                </headerToolbar>
                <columns>
                    <Column><Text text="Employee ID" /></Column>
                    <Column><Text text="Employee Name" /></Column>
                    <Column><Text text="Department" /></Column>
                </columns>
                <items>
                    <ColumnListItem>
                        <cells>
                            <Text text="{EmployeeId}" />
                            <Text text="{EmployeeName}" />
                            <Text text="{Department}" />
                        </cells>
                    </ColumnListItem>
                </items>
            </Table>
        </content>
    </Page>
</mvc:View>

The table binds to a model collection named Employees. The button invokes the controller method onExportExcel.

4. Configure the SAPUI5 export library

Declare the export library in the sap.ui5 section of manifest.json. Merge this dependency into your existing configuration rather than replacing other dependencies.

{
  "sap.ui5": {
    "dependencies": {
      "libs": {
        "sap.m": {},
        "sap.ui.core": {},
        "sap.ui.export": {}
      }
    }
  }
}

5. Implement Excel export in the controller

The following controller example defines the export columns explicitly, so only the selected fields are included in the Excel file.

sap.ui.define([
    "sap/ui/core/mvc/Controller",
    "sap/ui/export/Spreadsheet",
    "sap/m/MessageBox"
], function (Controller, Spreadsheet, MessageBox) {
    "use strict";

    return Controller.extend("demo.controller.Employee", {
        onExportExcel: async function () {
            const oTable = this.byId("employeeTable");
            const oBinding = oTable.getBinding("items");

            if (!oBinding) {
                MessageBox.error("Unable to retrieve the table data.");
                return;
            }

            const aContexts = oBinding.getContexts(
                0,
                oBinding.getLength()
            );

            const aData = aContexts.map(function (oContext) {
                return oContext.getObject();
            });

            if (!aData.length) {
                MessageBox.information(
                    "There is no data available to export."
                );
                return;
            }

            const aColumns = [
                {
                    label: "Employee ID",
                    property: "EmployeeId",
                    type: "string"
                },
                {
                    label: "Employee Name",
                    property: "EmployeeName",
                    type: "string"
                },
                {
                    label: "Department",
                    property: "Department",
                    type: "string"
                }
            ];

            const oSpreadsheet = new Spreadsheet({
                workbook: { columns: aColumns },
                dataSource: aData,
                fileName: "Employee_Overview.xlsx"
            });

            try {
                await oSpreadsheet.build();
            } catch (oError) {
                MessageBox.error(
                    "Excel export failed. Please try again."
                );
            } finally {
                oSpreadsheet.destroy();
            }
        }
    });
});

How the code works

  • Table binding: Retrieves data associated with the table's item binding.
  • Column definitions: Specifies the Excel header and corresponding model property.
  • Data source: Supplies row objects to the spreadsheet generator.
  • File name: Sets the downloaded workbook's name.
  • Build and cleanup: Generates the workbook and destroys the spreadsheet instance afterward.

Note: This example is intended for a client-side collection whose required data is available in the binding. For large OData datasets, server-side paging, or growing tables, make sure all required records are fetched before exporting. The currently rendered rows may not represent the complete dataset.

6. Export only the required columns

A common issue is that the Excel file contains extra fields that are not intended for business users. This can happen when developers export entire model objects or derive columns from every property in the backend response.

For example, the backend may provide:

const oEmployee = {
    EmployeeId: "E1001",
    EmployeeName: "Alex Morgan",
    Department: "Finance",
    InternalReference: "REF-0048",
    CreatedBy: "TECH_USER"
};

If business users need only three fields, define only those fields in the export configuration:

const aColumns = [
    {
        label: "Employee ID",
        property: "EmployeeId",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: "Employee Name",
        property: "EmployeeName",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: "Department",
        property: "Department",
        type: "string"
    }
];

Only the properties listed in the export configuration are included. Backend-only fields such as InternalReference and CreatedBy are excluded.

7. Keep Excel headers consistent with the UI

Excel headers should be meaningful to end users rather than exposing technical property names.

UI column header Model property Excel header
Employee IDEmployeeIdEmployee ID
Employee NameEmployeeNameEmployee Name
DepartmentDepartmentDepartment

The label property determines the Excel header, while property identifies the source field.

For multilingual applications, labels can be retrieved from the i18n resource bundle:

const oBundle = this.getView()
    .getModel("i18n")
    .getResourceBundle();

const aColumns = [
    {
        label: oBundle.getText("employeeId"),
        property: "EmployeeId",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: oBundle.getText("employeeName"),
        property: "EmployeeName",
        type: "string"
    }
];

8. Export filtered or sorted table data

Applications often include search fields, status filters, and sorting options. Decide whether the export should contain the currently filtered data or the complete dataset.

For a client-side table binding, the binding can provide contexts for the current filter and sort configuration:

const oBinding = oTable.getBinding("items");

const aFilteredContexts = oBinding.getContexts(
    0,
    oBinding.getLength()
);

const aExportData = aFilteredContexts.map(function (oContext) {
    return oContext.getObject();
});

Pass the resulting objects to the spreadsheet as the data source. For server-side OData bindings, the number of records may be limited by paging or service configuration. To export every matching backend record, implement appropriate paging or a dedicated data-retrieval process.

9. Handle numbers and dates correctly

Choosing suitable data types helps Excel interpret values correctly.

const aColumns = [
    {
        label: "Employee ID",
        property: "EmployeeId",
        type: "string"
    },
    {
        label: "Monthly Salary",
        property: "MonthlySalary",
        type: "number"
    },
    {
        label: "Joining Date",
        property: "JoiningDate",
        type: "date"
    }
];

Use string for identifiers that may contain leading zeros, number for numeric values, and date for valid date values. Verify supported types and formatting options for your SAPUI5 version.

10. Common issues and troubleshooting

Issue Recommended check
Export button does nothingVerify the event handler name and browser console errors.
Excel contains extra columnsReview the explicit workbook column definition.
Headers show technical namesSet the intended user-facing label for every column.
Some records are missingCheck binding length, paging, growing behavior, and OData retrieval.
Dates or numbers are incorrectVerify model data types and spreadsheet column configuration.
Export fails in the browserCheck library availability, SAPUI5 version compatibility, and console errors.

Conclusion

The sap.ui.export.Spreadsheet API provides a practical way to add Excel export to freestyle SAPUI5 applications. The most important considerations are to define the required columns explicitly, use meaningful labels, handle the table's actual data binding correctly, and account for filtering and server-side paging.

Following these practices helps deliver clean, consistent Excel files that meet business users' reporting needs.
